html:
The Nahua of Guerrero are Nahuatl-speaking communities of the mountains and the Balsas River valley in central Guerrero, southern Mexico. In the 1400s Nahua towns here lived alongside Tlapanec, Mixtec and Chontal peoples.

In the late 1400s the Aztec Triple Alliance conquered the region and made provinces such as Tepecoacuilco, which paid tribute in cotton cloth and other goods listed in the Codex Mendoza. The Spanish took over in the 1520s, and nearby Taxco became a great silver mining town. Nahua villages of Guerrero still speak Nahuatl and are known for paintings on amate bark paper and for the lacquer work of Olinalá. See also Nahuas.
